title: Water all through it
hook: rain, springs, rivers of the garden: water as mercy all through the book

segments.voice: Yesterday: ayah, and your line, the world is signs. Today, one sign that runs through the whole book like a river.

Turn on a tap. It's the most forgettable act of the day: brushing teeth, filling a kettle, rinsing a cup. The Qur'an was first heard in the Hijaz, where a well could decide whether a town existed, and a caravan's route ran from one water source to the next. There, water isn't background. It's life and death. And it flows through the book, from the making of living things to its pictures of the Garden.
screen: `A LAND WHERE A WELL MAKES A TOWN.`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning of things. Surah twenty-one says Allah made every living thing from water. Surah eleven pictures His throne upon the water before the heavens and earth were made. Then the rain. Surah seven describes the winds sent ahead as good news, going before His mercy, and that mercy is the rain: clouds driven to a dead land, and out of it every kind of fruit. Rain and mercy share a sentence. Springs burst from rock when Musa strikes it with his staff, twelve of them, one for each tribe. And at the far end of the book, the Garden is again and again called gardens beneath which rivers flow; surah forty-seven names rivers of water that never goes stale. Water is in the daily life of the faith too. No prayer without washing first, the wudu: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet. And a detail that surprises people: a hadith in al-Bukhari says the Prophet ﷺ would do his whole wudu with about one mudd of water, roughly two cupped handfuls, and bathe with a few times that. Another hadith, in Abu Dawud, says Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. So water in Islamic teaching is a mercy from above, a trust held in common, and something not to be poured away. The same tradition that promises rivers remembers a Prophet who used a handful well.

Hold a glass of water, or picture one, and look at it before you drink: a cloud, a river, a reservoir, a pipe someone laid. Then drink slowly, in small sips, with a breath between each. If you'd like, begin as Muslims are taught to, with bismillah, and finish with alhamdulillah.
Wudu. The washing before prayer, hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, feet, done by the Prophet with about two cupped handfuls of water. Today's word.
Your line: water is mercy. About two handfuls, used well, were enough for him. Day six hundred seventy.

screen: `DAY 670 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MARYAM, THE ONLY WOMAN NAMED.`

howItsDone: Muslims wash with water (wudu) before prayer and are taught to use little of it, following hadith about the Prophet's small measure; saying bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after is a common practice.
